title: An interpersonally comparable, preference-respecting measure of welfare

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a validated way to measure how well different people are doing while respecting each person's own preferences. It would produce a cardinal index: a measure with an explicit interpretation of welfare levels and differences, rather than simply an ordering from better to worse. Its scale would have a reproducible basis that permits meaningful comparisons across people, so that changing an arbitrary personal reporting scale would not change the conclusions.

Existing equivalence approaches provide a conceptual starting point. They associate a person's actual situation with a specified reference situation that the person considers equally good. Equivalent income expresses such a comparison in income terms under reference conditions. This can preserve individual preferences while supplying a common basis for comparison. The missing advance is convincing empirical validation and workable implementation of comparable welfare measurement, rather than the invention of preference-based frameworks from scratch.

A measure of individual welfare and a rule for combining welfare across society are separate components. Even a successful individual measure would need an explicit social aggregation rule before it could assign a single ranking to policies that benefit some people and harm others. The innovation would make the information entering that judgment more defensible; it would not determine every ethical choice involved in the judgment.

significance.text: Policies commonly create winners and losers. If those policies are to receive a single welfare ranking, their evaluation needs a basis for comparing gains and losses across people. Conditional on establishing valid interpersonal comparability, this innovation could substantially improve the empirical foundation of those comparisons. It could make welfare accounts and evaluations of real reforms more reproducible, with transparent explanations for why their conclusions differ from GDP rankings. Broader welfare measures already depart from GDP; the additional advance would be validated preference respect and interpersonal comparability.

GDP and national income are economic accounting aggregates, not welfare measures constructed from an assumed utility function. A comparable welfare index could complement those accounts by making the treatment of dimensions such as leisure, mortality and distribution explicit. Its policy conclusions would nevertheless remain conditional on reference situations, the treatment of preferences and the chosen aggregation rule. Fleurbaey's lecture specifically identifies inequality aversion in social aggregation as an ethical parameter. Better measurement would therefore support evidence-informed judgments without making policy rankings purely empirical facts.

Arrow's theorem supplies relevant context. For more than two alternatives, its ordinal framework cannot simultaneously satisfy unrestricted domain, social ordering, weak Pareto, nondictatorship and independence of irrelevant alternatives. Interpersonally comparable cardinal information changes the informational basis and opens additional aggregation possibilities; cardinality by itself is insufficient. A successful welfare measure would thus expand the information available for social evaluation, rather than refute the theorem. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy also describes other ways to relax Arrow's framework, so this metric is not the only route to useful social evaluation.

Conditional downstream possibilities include comparable national welfare accounts and more consistent appraisal of reforms with effects across several dimensions of life. These applications would still require separate principles for policies that change people's preferences, affect future generations or extend across centuries under deep uncertainty. This is an enabling measurement advance, not a complete solution to social choice or long-term policy evaluation. No supplied historical calibration supports a precise analogy with a particular past scientific breakthrough.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is to validate an explicit interpersonal scale while preserving each person's assessment of their own circumstances. Within-person preference rankings do not automatically specify the size of welfare differences or make those differences comparable across people. Arrow's exclusion of interpersonal comparisons is an informational restriction of his framework, not a demonstration that every possible interpersonal comparison is meaningless.

Self-reported well-being presents a measurement barrier because people can use response scales differently and interpret questions differently. Identical answers need not establish identical welfare, and different answers need not establish a corresponding interpersonal welfare gap. Fleurbaey's lecture identifies reporting heterogeneity as a difficulty for interpersonal comparison. This motivates validation of reporting scales; it does not establish that all self-report measures fail.

Preference-based equivalence measures require information about individual circumstances and preferences over the dimensions included in the evaluation. Fleurbaey describes these approaches as demanding in data and describes individual preference elicitation as unsatisfactory. The implementation challenge includes obtaining adequate dimensional coverage and reliable preference information at practical survey cost. The supplied evidence does not establish that every implementation must separately elicit willingness to pay for every non-income dimension, or demonstrate the extent of disagreement among elicitation methods.

A further validation problem is distinguishing genuine measurement from agreement produced by shared assumptions. Two methods can generate identical policy rankings while assigning incompatible welfare levels or differences, and methods can agree because they share a bias. A convincing advance must therefore identify which scale transformations preserve meaning, explain its reference choices and test more than rank concordance. These are methodological requirements proposed for this innovation, rather than a claim that an accepted validation protocol already exists.

current_state.text: Charles I. Jones and Peter J. Klenow's September 2016 American Economic Review article, Beyond GDP? Welfare across Countries and Time, proposes a welfare statistic incorporating consumption, leisure, mortality and inequality. Its abstract reports a high correlation with GDP per capita alongside often-large deviations. This establishes an existing example of broader welfare accounting. The supplied review had access to the article's landing page and abstract, not the full article, so that evidence does not establish the specific consumption-equivalence construction or assumed common utility function described in the earlier research.

The earlier research attributed a median deviation of about 35 percent across 13 countries to an open reproduction of the Jones–Klenow article. No text of that reproduction was captured for the supplied review, and the retained abstract does not verify either the sample count or the statistic. Those figures remain an unverified attribution rather than an established result in this record. The access limitation does not show that they are false.

Benjamin and coauthors' What Do Happiness Data Mean? Theory and Survey Evidence, available here as a May 2021 revised NBER working paper, examines how subjective well-being questions relate to commonly assumed utility notions. On average across respondents, the studied measures did not closely match lifetime, forward-looking or flow utility. The study uses introspective survey evidence from a nonrepresentative US sample and cannot directly compare every reported well-being component with actual preference components. It supports caution about interpreting the studied happiness questions as utility, rather than a universal rejection of happiness data. The supplied extraction was truncated, although the relevant findings and methodological limitations were readable in the review.

Marc Fleurbaey's Social Welfare Beyond GDP lecture develops equivalence measures and describes an interpersonal Pareto property: when two people have identical preferences, their interpersonal comparison should agree with their common assessment of their relative situations. The lecture also qualifies the approach by dimensional coverage, demanding individual survey requirements and unsatisfactory preference elicitation. These are documented properties and limitations of an existing framework, not evidence that the proposed validated measurement capability has been achieved. October 2026 is the supplied file metadata date; the review did not establish an internal lecture date.

The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Arrow's theorem, substantively revised on 7 December 2025, documents both the ordinal impossibility result and the additional possibilities created by interpersonal comparability. It provides conceptual context rather than an empirical demonstration of a welfare metric. Taken together, the supplied sources establish useful frameworks and continuing measurement barriers. They do not establish an exhaustive account of research through 1 November 2026, because no freshness-search results were supplied.

The earlier research also mentioned a working paper attributed to Da Costa, Fleurbaey and coauthors, dated 9 December 2025, as reporting differences in willingness to pay across elicitation methods. Neither the paper nor its described secondary listing was supplied to the review, and no corresponding source URL was provided. Its findings and reported date therefore remain unassessed here.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scientific demonstration: specify the welfare construct, included dimensions, reference situations, admissible scale transformations and basis for interpersonal comparisons before testing. State the social aggregation rule separately, including any inequality-aversion parameters. This would make clear which conclusions depend on measurement and which depend on ethical choices. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established field standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed scientific demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Apply at least two independently designed elicitation methods to the same people. Using prespecified statistical tolerances and adequate precision, test equivalence of interpersonal welfare levels and differences as well as agreement on rankings of a prespecified set of real policies. Investigate shared assumptions and possible common biases. Ranking agreement alone would be insufficient to demonstrate a comparable cardinal scale.
completion_criteria.label: Apply at least two independently designed elicitation methods

completion_criteria.text: Test two distinct forms of preference consistency. First, within the declared scope, an evaluated policy change that every affected person prefers should receive the corresponding Pareto-consistent assessment. Second, for people with identical preferences, the interpersonal comparison of their situations should agree with their common ranking of those situations. The latter is the interpersonal Pareto property described in Fleurbaey's lecture; it is different from unanimous preference for a policy change.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility demonstration: publish elicitation instruments, estimation procedures, uncertainty estimates and sensitivity to reference situations, dimensional coverage and aggregation parameters. Independent teams should reproduce results and test them across declared populations and policy settings. Report survey burden, cost, missing-data effects and the circumstances in which the methods cease to agree. Finite testing would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility demonstration

completion_criteria.text: As an additional institutional milestone, produce an official welfare account alongside GDP in at least two countries with documented methods and uncertainty. The two-country threshold is a proposed adoption target, not scientific validation. A dashboard of separate indicators without a tested aggregation would not demonstrate the intended single-index capability; official adoption alone would not establish that the index measures welfare correctly.

related_concepts.text: ECO-03, A predictive and welfare-coherent theory of boundedly rational choice, has the closest conceptual overlap: interpreting observed choices and well-being reports affects which preferences a welfare measure should respect. The Benjamin working paper illustrates the difficulty of treating subjective well-being responses as utility. ECO-04 targets interpersonal measurement, while ECO-03 targets a theory of choice and its welfare interpretation. Only ECO-03's title and the research cross-reference were supplied, so a more detailed comparison remains unavailable.

Roster-based synthesis: ECO-02, Prospective transport of causal policy effects across populations, concerns predicting policy effects in a target population. ECO-08, Structural counterfactuals for macroeconomic regimes, concerns outcomes under alternative regimes. Both could supply consequences for ECO-04 to evaluate; neither title implies a solution to interpersonal welfare comparison. Conversely, a welfare index would not establish causal transportability or validate structural counterfactual predictions.

Roster-based synthesis: ECO-01, Empirically valid aggregate market laws beyond the Sonnenschein–Mantel–Debreu barrier, concerns reliable aggregate market behavior. ECO-07, A verified, manipulable law of sustained productivity growth, concerns explaining and influencing growth. ECO-04 could help evaluate the welfare consequences of their applications, but comparable welfare measurement would not by itself discover aggregate market laws or establish a law of productivity growth.

Roster-based synthesis: ECO-05, Approximately efficient voluntary provision of global public goods, and ECO-09, A general, detail-free allocation compiler for private-information economies, concern provision and allocation mechanisms. A welfare measure could inform their objectives or evaluation. It would not by itself supply incentives for voluntary cooperation, elicit private information strategically or implement an allocation.

Roster-based synthesis: ECO-06, Household-scale markets for national, occupational, and housing income risk, and ECO-10, Liquidity and credit without run-prone debt, concern financial arrangements. ECO-04 could help compare their consequences for different households under explicit distributional judgments. It remains distinct from building risk-sharing markets or designing stable liquidity and credit systems.

Equivalent-income and consumption-equivalent approaches are direct intellectual neighbors. The supplied Fleurbaey lecture develops preference-based reference comparisons, while the Jones–Klenow abstract establishes broader welfare accounting across several dimensions without verifying the detailed consumption-equivalence specification in the earlier research. Voting-rule design is another neighboring but distinct project: changing a ballot rule addresses aggregation of expressed preferences under a decision procedure, whereas ECO-04 seeks validated welfare information for interpersonal comparison.

change_log.change: Reframed the missing advance as validated, reproducible interpersonal measurement while retaining the original concept and ID.
change_log.reason: Existing equivalence frameworks already provide conceptual foundations; the evidence supports substantial implementation barriers without establishing that no framework exists.

change_log.change: Separated welfare measurement from social aggregation and corrected the treatment of GDP and national income.
change_log.reason: Accounting aggregates are not themselves utility-based welfare measures, and comparable measurement does not eliminate ethical choices such as inequality aversion.

change_log.change: Qualified the relationship to Arrow's theorem and included its more-than-two-alternatives scope.
change_log.reason: Interpersonally comparable information expands the informational framework rather than refuting the theorem or constituting its only possible relaxation.

change_log.change: Replaced the universal willingness-to-pay requirement and asserted elicitation-method disagreement with narrower data and elicitation barriers.
change_log.reason: The supplied lecture supports demanding preference information and unsatisfactory elicitation, but the retained evidence does not establish those stronger assertions.

change_log.change: Retained the 13-country, approximately 35-percent claim as an explicitly unverified attribution and qualified the consumption-equivalence and common-utility descriptions.
change_log.reason: The reproduction was not captured, and the reviewed AEA abstract does not establish those details. Missing evidence does not demonstrate falsity.

change_log.change: Narrowed the interpretation of Benjamin and coauthors' findings and identified the working-paper revision, sample and extraction limits.
change_log.reason: The evidence concerns particular questions and introspective responses in a nonrepresentative US sample, rather than all happiness data.

change_log.change: Preserved the lecture's interpersonal Pareto reasoning and distinguished supplied dating from internally established content.
change_log.reason: The framework's comparison principle is substantively useful, while October 2026 is metadata rather than a verified internal lecture date.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration to cover cardinal levels and differences, separate consistency tests, sensitivity, reproducibility and practical limits.
change_log.reason: Rank agreement cannot establish cardinal comparability, unanimous policy improvement differs from interpersonal Pareto, and official adoption is an institutional milestone.

change_log.change: Explained relationships to every other roster entry while distinguishing source-backed discussion from title-based synthesis.
change_log.reason: The roster supplies identities and titles, but not full concept records supporting detailed claims about their implementations.

change_log.reason: The review identified a source-identity mismatch for that PDF, and no first-pass assessment was supplied.

unresolved_issues: The 13-country, approximately 35-percent Jones–Klenow statistic, its precise definition and the detailed utility specification remain unverified within the supplied evidence.
The Da Costa, Fleurbaey and coauthors working paper, its reported 9 December 2025 date and its elicitation-method findings cannot be assessed without the paper or the referenced listing.
The supplied October 2026 date for Fleurbaey's lecture is not established by an internal date in the reviewed document.
No freshness-search results were supplied, so this record cannot establish an exhaustive research frontier as of 1 November 2026.
The target welfare construct, reference situations, legitimate interpersonal scale and acceptable statistical tolerances remain to be specified and validated.
How to handle changing preferences, future generations and deep long-term uncertainty remains unresolved by the proposed measurement advance.
Detailed comparison with ECO-03 and the other roster concepts is limited by the absence of their full records.
